claims.claim: A readiness-anchored invitation gives the prospective reader more useful thinking time than a display-anchored invitation.
Wait five seconds specifies one deadline without naming a starting event.
Repeating READY has no effect under a policy that restarts on every READY.
A canceled interval remains active until its original deadline under a cancel-clears-active policy.
A timer due at t=8 necessarily delivers output at t=8 when the next poll is t=10.
Two clocks with different offsets can be subtracted directly to recover elapsed time.
A negative remaining time must be displayed after a late poll.
Pausing and canceling have the same continuation rule in every timer.
An invitation sent twice necessarily represents two intended rounds.
Ignoring every READY after the first remains correct after explicit cancellation and a new-round request.
A displayed timestamp alone reveals whether it marks sending, receiving, or readiness.
Equal duration values guarantee equal opportunities to respond.
A response received after the deadline proves the reader chose it after the deadline.
The absence of READY is a negative answer to the lesson’s content question.
A shared countdown numeral alone identifies which of two concurrent rounds is active.
Replacing seconds with beats preserves every deadline without stating beat duration.
Canceling a timer also deletes every response already recorded in that round.
A named event is enough to compute a deadline when that event’s time was never observed.
